chunks.heading: Assessing the numerical error of a result
chunks.text:
How many digits of a computed result can be trusted, and where the error comes from. The methods below are those
`fobis assess` applies to a declared case, one per family of variants; each section names the method, its
assumptions and its references (full entries in the references document of this pack).

chunks.heading: Assessing the numerical error of a result > Significant digits of an ensemble
chunks.text:
Run the same computation several times with a perturbation that should not matter (another rounding, compiler,
thread count, input within its uncertainty) and look at the spread of a result `x` over the `n` members. With
mean `mu` and sample standard deviation `sigma`, the number of significant digits the members share is

```
s = -log10(sigma / |mu|)
```

the estimator of Monte Carlo arithmetic (Parker, Pierce and Eggert 2000), also used by Verificarlo. All members
equal means every digit is reproduced (`s` infinite); `mu = 0` makes `s` meaningless (0 reported): assess such a
quantity through a quantity that does not vanish, or by absolute difference.

`sigma` from a few members is itself uncertain. A one-sided 95% lower bound on `s` follows from the chi-square
upper bound of `sigma`, `sigma_up = sigma * sqrt(k / chi2(0.05, k))` with `k = n - 1` degrees of freedom
(exact quantiles for k = 1 and 2, the Wilson and Hilferty 1931 approximation above). With 3 members the bound is
far below the estimate; it tightens as members are added. The bound assumes independent random samples (Sohier
et al. 2021 discuss confidence intervals for stochastic arithmetic): for deterministic variants, such as
compiler flags, it is indicative only.

chunks.heading: Assessing the numerical error of a result > Precision family
chunks.text:
Rebuild with every real promoted to a wider kind and compare: the digits on which the normal build agrees with the
promoted one estimate the rounding error of the normal build (the promoted build serves as the more accurate
reference, `-log10(|x - x_ref| / |x_ref|)` per point). Measured: a single-precision sum agreed with its promoted
build to 2.0 digits.

Assumptions and limits: the promoted build must be much more accurate (its own rounding negligible), and
promotion must not change the program's logic. Promotion flags cover different declarations per compiler
(compilers pack): a code with a kind module is promoted by changing the kind parameter. Promotion changes binary
record lengths and integer storage tricks: measured, blanket 128-bit promotion broke PENF (`storage_size` stored
into an `integer(1)` parameter).

chunks.heading: Assessing the numerical error of a result > Rounding family
chunks.text:
Rebuild with flags that change rounding without changing the algorithm: optimisation levels, FMA contraction on
and off, value-unsafe math, vectorisation off. The spread over these members is a cheap, deterministic stand-in
for stochastic arithmetic: it shows how sensitive the result is to the order and fusion of operations, but it
samples a few rounding patterns, not a distribution. Monte Carlo arithmetic (Verificarlo: Denis, de Oliveira
Castro and Petit 2016) and discrete stochastic arithmetic (CADNA: Jézéquel and Chesneaux 2008) perturb every
operation randomly and give a statistically founded estimate; use them when the result matters and they are
available.

Measured: a compensated (Kahan) sum kept every printed digit in every member except `-ffast-math`, which removes
the compensation (Kahan 1965; compilers pack); in FOODIE an exact floating-point equality test
(`final_time - int(final_time/Dt)*Dt == 0`) failed under FMA contraction.

chunks.heading: Assessing the numerical error of a result > Compiler family
chunks.text:
Build and run the case with the project's other modes (other compilers). Differences in the last digits come
from contraction, reassociation and intrinsic implementations; differences in leading digits from bugs: a
compiler-dependent behaviour (uninitialised variables, aliasing violations, argument mismatches) or a compiler
bug. Rebuild with value-safe flags on every compiler to separate the two (compilers pack, comparison).

chunks.heading: Assessing the numerical error of a result > Parallel family
chunks.text:
Run with several thread and rank counts, and repeat each. Results that differ between repeats at the same count
are non-deterministic: an unordered floating-point reduction (OpenMP `atomic` or `reduction`, `MPI_Allreduce`
with a varying algorithm) sums in a different order each run. Measured: an OpenMP `atomic` reduction gave
repeats differing by about 3e-5 relative at 4 threads and identical results at 1 thread. Results that differ
between counts but repeat exactly come from a count-dependent order of operations (decomposition-dependent
sums), or from a race that a different count exposes. Bitwise reproducibility needs a fixed reduction order or a
reproducible summation algorithm (Demmel and Nguyen 2015).

chunks.heading: Assessing the numerical error of a result > Inputs family
chunks.text:
Perturb declared inputs and measure the response. One at a time (each parameter low and high around its
nominal value, the others fixed) gives the elasticity

```
E = ((q_high - q_low) / q0) / ((p_high - p_low) / p0)
```

the relative change of the output per relative change of the input: |E| > 1 amplifies the input's uncertainty.
Measured: for `k^2 exp(-dt)` the elasticities were 2 for `k` and -0.5 for `dt`, the analytic values (`2` and
`-dt` at the nominal `dt = 0.5`). One-at-a-time analysis misses interactions between parameters (Saltelli et al.
2008). Sampling all inputs from their distributions (Monte Carlo) gives the output's spread, with a standard
error decreasing as 1/sqrt(N), and correlations between each input and the output. Measured: a Monte Carlo
standard deviation of 6.1 % matched first-order propagation of the input uncertainty.

chunks.heading: Assessing the numerical error of a result > Refinement family
chunks.text:
Run the case at three or more levels of a resolution parameter `h` (grid spacing, time step, tolerance) and
measure how a scalar result converges. With levels 3 (coarse), 2, 1 (fine), refinement ratios `r21 = h2/h1`,
`r32 = h3/h2` and differences `e21 = f2 - f1`, `e32 = f3 - f2`:

- ratio `R = e21/e32`: `0 < R < 1` monotonic convergence, `-1 < R < 0` oscillatory, `|R| >= 1` divergent
  (Stern et al. 2001);
- observed order `p` by fixed-point iteration on `p = |ln|e32/e21| + q(p)| / ln r21`,
  `q(p) = ln((r21^p - s)/(r32^p - s))`, `s = sign(e32/e21)` (Celik et al. 2008; with a constant ratio `q = 0`);
- Richardson extrapolation `f_ext = (r21^p f1 - f2) / (r21^p - 1)` (Richardson 1911) and the error estimate
  `|f_ext - f1|`;
- Grid Convergence Index of the fine level `GCI = 1.25 |e21/f1| / (r21^p - 1)` (Roache 1994; factor 1.25 for
  three or more levels).

These hold only in the asymptotic range, where the leading error term dominates. With four or more levels FoBiS
compares the orders of the last two triples and calls the study asymptotic when they agree within 10% (a FoBiS
criterion, not a standard one); otherwise the order is reported as not converged rather than as a property of
the method. Measured: trapezoid rule for the integral of `exp(x)` on [0, 1], order 2.000, the extrapolated value
equal to the exact `e - 1` to 9 digits and the error estimate equal to the true error; RK4 4.06; FOODIE's schemes 1.012 (explicit Euler), 2.016, 3.016 (SSP Runge-Kutta 2 and 3), 4.012 (SSP-RK(5,4)).
Oberkampf and Roy (2010) treat code and solution verification at length.

chunks.heading: Assessing the numerical error of a result > Budgets
chunks.text:
A budget states what a result must achieve: `digits >= 6`, `order >= 1.9`, `error <= 1e-4`. Choosing it from the
assessment, not before it, keeps it honest: the measured digits of the normal build bound what any tolerance
on the result can promise. A `fobis verify` tolerance tighter than the assessed digits fails on harmless
changes (another compiler, thread count); a looser one hides real changes.

chunks.heading: Floating-point facts behind result differences
chunks.text:
Why the same algorithm gives different numbers, and how to compare numbers that are allowed to differ.
References are listed in full in the references document of this pack.

chunks.heading: Floating-point facts behind result differences > Rounding and the order of operations
chunks.text:
Every floating-point operation rounds its exact result to the nearest representable number (IEEE 754 default
rounding); the relative error of one operation is at most the unit roundoff `u` (2^-24 for 32-bit reals, 2^-53
for 64-bit reals). Addition is therefore not associative: `(a + b) + c` and `a + (b + c)` can differ. Any change
of the order of a sum (vectorisation, a parallel reduction, another compiler's reassociation, a loop
reordering) changes the result within the error bound of the sum, not exactly (Goldberg 1991).

For recursive summation of `n` terms the error bound grows with `n`: `|computed - exact| <= gamma(n-1) * sum|x_i|`
with `gamma(k) = k u / (1 - k u)` (Higham 2002, chapter 4). The bound depends on `sum|x_i|`, not on the sum:
when terms cancel, the relative error of the result can be large.

chunks.heading: Floating-point facts behind result differences > Compensated summation
chunks.text:
Kahan's compensated summation (Kahan 1965) carries the rounding error of each addition in a correction term and
reduces the bound to about `2u sum|x_i|`, independent of `n` to first order (Higham 2002). It relies on the exact
order of operations: `c = (t - s) - y` is zero in exact arithmetic, so a compiler allowed to reassociate removes
it. Measured: gfortran `-ffast-math`, ifx at its default `-fp-model fast=1`, and ifx `-fp-model fast=2` removed
the compensation; gfortran `-O2`/`-O3`, ifx `-fp-model precise` and nvfortran `-O2`/`-fast` kept it (compilers
pack). Every error-free transformation (TwoSum, TwoProduct, double-double arithmetic) has the same requirement.

chunks.heading: Floating-point facts behind result differences > Fused multiply-add
chunks.text:
An FMA computes `a*b + c` with one rounding instead of two. It is usually more accurate, but it changes results,
and it breaks code that relies on two roundings: `a*b - a*b` contracted on one side is not 0 (it is the rounding
error of the product), and an expression symmetric in exact arithmetic can become asymmetric. Whether a compiler
contracts depends on its defaults and the target instruction set (compilers pack, comparison): a new `-march`
or a new compiler can change the last digits without any source change.

chunks.heading: Floating-point facts behind result differences > NaN, Inf and value-unsafe modes
chunks.text:
Under "finite math" assumptions (gfortran `-ffast-math`/`-ffinite-math-only`, ifx `-fp-model fast=2`) the
compiler may delete tests for NaN: measured, `ieee_is_nan(x)` and `x /= x` returned false for a NaN. A code that
checks its results for NaN must be built without these modes, or keep the check in a file compiled without
them. Flush-to-zero modes (nvfortran `-Mflushz`, part of `-fast`) replace subnormal results by zero, which
changes results that pass through very small values.

chunks.heading: Floating-point facts behind result differences > Comparing results with a tolerance
chunks.text:
Bitwise equality is the right test only for results that must be reproducible exactly (same build, same
inputs, deterministic code). Otherwise compare with a tolerance stated for each quantity:

- absolute `|a - b| <= A`: for quantities that are near zero or have a natural scale;
- relative `|a - b| <= R |ref|`: for quantities far from zero; meaningless where `ref` vanishes;
- in units in the last place (ulp): the number of representable values between `a` and `b`, independent of
  magnitude; a few ulp absorb the reordering of a short computation, not of a long one.

`fobis verify` accepts `abs A rel R ulp N` per quantity (`|a - b| <= A + R |ref|`, or within N ulp); NaN equals
NaN and infinities compare by equality. Derive the tolerance from an assessment of the result (assessment
document) rather than guessing it: the digits that survive harmless perturbations are what a tolerance can
check.

chunks.heading: Floating-point facts behind result differences > Reproducibility across runs
chunks.text:
A deterministic serial program, built once, gives bitwise-identical results on the same machine unless a
library it calls chooses its code path at run time. Parallel programs do so only when every reduction has a
fixed order: OpenMP `reduction` and `atomic` updates, MPI reductions and GPU atomics do not guarantee one.
Measured: an OpenMP `atomic` sum differed between repeats at 4 threads. `fobis verify --repeat N` checks that N
runs agree exactly before a reference is written; reproducible reduction algorithms exist (Demmel and Nguyen
2015) at extra cost.

chunks.heading: Measuring run time
chunks.text:
How to decide whether a change made a program faster, slower, or neither. These are the statistics `fobis bench`
applies; references are listed in full in the references document of this pack.

chunks.heading: Measuring run time > Use the median and its interval
chunks.text:
Run times are skewed: most runs cluster near a minimum, and interference (other processes, frequency changes,
page cache) adds a long tail of slow runs. The mean and a normal confidence interval assume a symmetric
distribution; the median does not. A distribution-free confidence interval of the median comes from order
statistics: with the `n` times sorted, the interval `[t(k), t(n+1-k)]` covers the median with probability at
least 95% for the largest `k` with `P(Binomial(n, 1/2) < k) <= 0.025` (Conover 1999). Below 6 runs no such
interval exists at 95%: the minimum number of runs is a property of the statistics, not a choice.

Report the median with its interval and the spread (median absolute deviation), not the best run: the best run
is the least representative one (Hoefler and Belli 2015 give twelve rules for reporting performance).

chunks.heading: Measuring run time > Compare interleaved, decide by the intervals
chunks.text:
Run the two versions alternately (A, B, A, B, ...) rather than all of A then all of B: slow drifts of the
machine (thermal throttling, a job starting elsewhere) then affect both. Call a version faster only when the two
median intervals do not overlap; the speedup `old/new` then lies in `[old.low/new.high, old.high/new.low]`.
Overlapping intervals mean "no measurable difference with these runs": more runs narrow the intervals, and
`fobis bench` keeps running until the relative half-width of each interval is below the declared target (default
2%) or a run or time limit is reached.

Measured: a memory-bound loop with one more statement gave medians of 0.131 s and 0.141 s and a speedup interval
of [0.827, 1.121], which contains 1: no measurable difference, although the medians differ by 8%.

chunks.heading: Measuring run time > Conditions that invalidate a measurement
chunks.text:
- Very short runs: below about 10 ms the program's start-up (loader, runtime initialisation, MPI start) is a
  large part of the time; measure a larger problem or time the kernel inside the program.
- A loaded machine: a load average above half the cores means the runs compete for processors and memory
  bandwidth; the intervals widen and the medians move. Note the load with the result.
- Warm-up: the first run pays for page faults, file cache misses and, on GPUs, context creation and code
  loading; discard it.
- GPU timing: device work is asynchronous. A host timer around a kernel launch measures the launch, not the
  kernel, unless the code waits for the device before reading the timer (hpc-practice pack, GPU benchmark
  timing). Consumer GPUs run 64-bit arithmetic at a small fraction of their 32-bit rate (hpc-practice pack).
- Different machines, compilers or modes: comparing against history is meaningful only for the same CPU, core
  count, GPU models, compiler and version, and mode.

chunks.heading: Measuring run time > CPU time versus wall time
chunks.text:
The CPU time of the child processes (`getrusage`) divided by the wall time shows how parallel a run was: about 1
for a serial program, about the thread count for a well-parallelised OpenMP run, much less when threads wait.
Measured on WSL2: serial programs showed a ratio of about 1.04, from accounting granularity (confirmed with
`/usr/bin/time`), not from parallelism.
